items.prompt: A user adds A (id 1) and B (id 2), deletes B, exits, restarts the app and adds C. Which id does C get?
items.answer: Id 3, from the next-id watermark saved in the file header
distractors: Id 2, from the highest surviving id plus one at the restart
Id 1, as numbering starts again after every restart
Id 2, as deleted ids are put back into a free list
items.explanation: addTask takes the id from snapshot.nextId(), and encode writes that watermark on the header line next to the revision. Deleting B leaves the watermark at 3, so C is "Task 3 added and saved." (reproduced). Nothing recomputes it from the surviving ids or keeps a free list.

items.prompt: A file in the original key=value format holds two complete tasks with ids 2 and 5. The user starts the app and adds a task. Which id does it get?
items.answer: Id 6, one above the highest legacy id that was loaded
distractors: Id 3, which is the first free gap after the lowest legacy id
Id 1, as a converted file then starts a completely fresh count
Id 3, as it is the number of tasks plus one
items.explanation: The legacy format has no watermark, so legacy() computes next = max(id) + 1 = 6 and builds the snapshot with it (reproduced: "Task 6 added and saved."). From then on the TODOLIST1 header keeps the watermark.

items.prompt: The app is started with a file name that does not exist yet. The user lists tasks and chooses 5. What is on disk afterwards?
items.answer: Nothing; the file is first written by an accepted change
distractors: An empty TODOLIST1 file, written out when the session ends
An empty TODOLIST1 file, written as soon as it loads
A lock file and an empty task file next to each other
items.explanation: bytes() returns null for a missing file and load() treats that as an empty snapshot without writing. Only save writes, and only a mutation calls it; listing and exiting never do (reproduced: no file existed afterwards; the unit test "missing file loads without creating data" checks the same).

items.prompt: A user picks 4, enters task id 1, and at "Type DELETE:" types delete in lowercase. What happens?
items.answer: It prints "Deletion cancelled." and task 1 stays saved
distractors: It deletes task 1, since the confirmation ignores case
It asks again until DELETE is typed in capital letters
It prints "Change not accepted:" and the reason for it
items.explanation: App compares the stripped answer with equals("DELETE"), which is case-sensitive; any other text takes the else branch and prints "Deletion cancelled." without calling deleteTask (reproduced). There is no retry loop.

items.prompt: A user picks 1 and types a title, and then the input ends before the description is entered. What happens?
items.answer: It reports the command was not applied, and the file is unchanged
distractors: The task is added with an empty description, and then the app exits
It crashes with a NoSuchElementException and a full stack trace
The task is kept in memory, and saved by the exit code afterwards too
items.explanation: line() throws NoSuchElementException when there is no next line, so addTask is never called. run() catches it and prints "Input ended; incomplete command was not applied." and the finally block only closes the scanner (reproduced: the file bytes were identical before and after).

items.prompt: Task 1 is already completed. The user picks 3 and enters 1 again. What happens?
items.answer: It prints "Task state accepted." but no new version is saved
distractors: It prints "Change not accepted:" as the task is already done
It saves version 3 with a fresh completion timestamp on it
It flips the task back to open, as option 3 toggles the state
items.explanation: withCompletion returns the same object when the requested state equals the current one, and setCompleted returns early when replacement == old, so commit and save are skipped. App still prints its success line (reproduced: the file was byte-for-byte unchanged). Reopening is option 7.

items.prompt: A task is added (version 1), edited once, completed with option 3, then reopened with option 7. How does option 2 show it?
items.answer: [ ] ID 1 / v4 with no Completed line, as reopening clears it
distractors: [ ] ID 1 / v2, as completing and reopening do not count as edits
[X] ID 1 / v4, as option 7 keeps the task marked as completed
[ ] ID 1 / v4 with the old Completed time still listed below it
items.explanation: edit and each real withCompletion change build a new Task with nextVersion(), so add, edit, complete and reopen give versions 1 to 4. Reopening passes null as completedAt, and the display adds a Completed line only for completed tasks (reproduced: "[ ] ID 1 / v4 - X2").

items.prompt: A user picks 6 for task 1 and presses Enter at both "New title:" and "New description:". What happens?
items.answer: The edit is rejected for its title, and the file stays the same
distractors: The title is kept and only the description is cleared and saved
Both fields are cleared, and the empty task is saved as v2
The edit is skipped, since nothing typed differs from before
items.explanation: Task.edit builds a new Task, and its text() check requires 1..160 characters for the title, so a blank title throws IllegalArgumentException before commit. App prints "Change not accepted: Title must contain 1..160 characters without controls." (reproduced; the file was unchanged). A blank description alone is allowed and clears it.

items.prompt: An add fails inside save because the atomic move throws. What do the file and the manager hold afterwards?
items.answer: The old file bytes, and only the tasks accepted before it
distractors: The old file bytes, but the manager lists the new task too
A partly written file that the next start then cannot parse
The new file, but the manager still lists the old tasks
items.explanation: commit calls repository.save first and assigns snapshot = candidate only after it returns; the temp file is deleted in finally and the target was never replaced. The test "atomic replacement failure retains memory and disk" checks both the bytes and getAllTasks (it passed when run).

items.prompt: Sessions A and B load the same empty file. A adds a task. B then tries to add a different task, is refused, and lists tasks. What does B show?
items.answer: "No matching tasks.", as B still holds its old snapshot
distractors: A's task only, as the failed save re-read the current file
Both tasks, as B keeps its own task in memory as a draft
B's own task only, as the add was applied before saving
items.explanation: B's commit throws during save before snapshot = candidate, and nothing reloads automatically, so B keeps the empty snapshot it loaded. Listing an empty snapshot prints "No matching tasks." (reproduced with two JVMs). Only option 9 re-reads the file.

items.prompt: After that refusal, session B chooses 9 (Reload) and enters its task again. What happens?
items.answer: It is accepted as task 2, and both tasks are listed
distractors: It is refused again until session A has been closed
It is accepted as task 1, which replaces A's task
It is accepted, but only B lists it until A reloads
items.explanation: reload() replaces B's baseline and snapshot with the current file, which holds A's task and a watermark of 2. The new add builds revision 2 on top of that and the byte comparison now matches, so "Task 2 added and saved." and the list shows both (reproduced). The lock is only held during a save.

items.prompt: At "Status (all/open/done):" a user types Done with a capital D. What happens?
items.answer: It prints "Change not accepted: Invalid search or status."
distractors: It lists the completed tasks whose text matches the search
It treats any status it does not know as all, and lists them
It asks again until one of the three lowercase words is typed
items.explanation: search checks List.of("all", "open", "done").contains(status), an exact, case-sensitive match, and throws IllegalArgumentException otherwise; the menu catch prints it (reproduced). The search text is lower-cased, but the status is not.

items.front: Why is Task immutable, and what does an edit return?
items.back: If a manager hands out mutable tasks, a caller can change them without validation or saving. Task has only final fields; edit and withCompletion build a new Task instead of changing the old one, and the constructor re-runs all validation. The service decides whether that replacement becomes accepted state.

items.front: Atomic replacement and stale-write detection solve different problems. What does each one prevent?
items.back: Writing a complete temporary file and atomically moving it over the target means a reader never sees half a snapshot. It does not show whether the candidate was built from an old read; detecting that needs a comparison against what this session loaded, done under a lock.

items.front: What is the tasks.txt.lock file next to the data file for?
items.back: It is the object the cooperative file lock is taken on during a save, so participating processes take turns. The app keeps it on disk; do not delete it while sessions are running. Programs that ignore the lock are not protected by it.
